title: The Amityville Horror
full_review:
At one point in "The Amityville Horror" (MGM), new homeowner George Lutz (Ryan Reynolds) tells his wife, Kathy (Melissa George), "There are no bad houses, just bad people." There are, however, bad movies, and this happens to be one of them.

The schlocky and unnecessarily grisly remake of the 1979 horror film is based on the alleged true experiences of a Long Island, N.Y., family who move into a spooky Dutch colonial house with a suspicious asking price and an evil past.

One year earlier, Ronald DeFeo Jr. (Brendan Donaldson), the eldest son of the house's previous owners, had, by maleficent mandate, slaughtered his parents and four siblings in their beds with a shotgun. The horrific crime, which made headlines at the time it was committed in 1974, is detailed in the film's disturbingly intense opening sequence.

Before you can say "caveat emptor" (Latin for "buyer beware"), strange things start to happen. Things start going bump in the night. Walls start to bleed. Young daughter
Chelsea's (Chloe Grace Moretz) ghostly playmate invites her to jump off the roof. And George starts to loose it, assuming the murderous glare and penchant for axes of Jack Nicholson in "The Shining."

Unlike the 1979 film, which starred James Brolin and Margot Kidder, the new version relies less on suspense than on haunted-house cliches and supernatural special effects and slick MTV-style editing. The creaky script also has a silly subplot involving an Indian graveyard -- a la "Poltergeist" -- and the lurking presence of a sadistic 17th-century missionary not in the earlier movie.

By the time Kathy does enlist the help of a local priest (Philip Baker Hall), viewers may wonder if the demonic voice yelling "Get out!" during the exorcism is, in fact, wise advice meant for them.

Directed by Andrew Douglas, whose past music-video experience is clearly evident in the film, "Amityville" has a few genuine jolts but ultimately unravels into a muddled stew of sensory overload and confusion.

The scariest thing about "Amityville" is that it is the last major film made by MGM -- the studio that made such classics as "The Wizard of Oz," "Ben-Hur," and "Singing in the Rain" -- before its recent purchase by the Sony Corp.

It's a pity that the MGM lion will go out with a whimper, not a roar.

The film has strong gratuitous violence and gore, torture images, a sexual encounter with shadowy nudity, several scenes of child peril, brief drug content and recurring rough language and profanity. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is O -- morally offensive. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is R -- restricted.
